story_text.value:
Saw HackerBooks shared the other day (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50326821) and wanted the same thing for books mentioned in popular podcasts instead.

As an avid reader and lover of podcasts, I always found it super interesting to hear about the books that helped shape influential people.

So I built PodBookCase (well Claude did) – a searchable directory of books mentioned across popular podcast episodes, using parsed transcript data (which I'll shortly make available)

I originally wanted to build it for myself, as I keep accumulating podcasts I want to watch and books I want to read. But then I thought it might be useful to other curious readers too.

title.value: Show HN: PodBookCase – Discover books mentioned on popular podcast episodes

story_text.value:
My brother and I run a 2-person lab that trains our own generative video models from scratch. The ultimate goal is a set of creative tools that make it easier for anyone to make animation.

Video models today are too slow/expensive and lack sufficient controls. Creativity is an iterative process. You make, you tweak, you get better. In our opinion, they're not usable yet for storytelling.

When we set out to build Linum v3 (our next video model) earlier this year, the primary goal was to bring the cost envelope of inference down significantly. If our model is fast and cheap, it's the first step (of many) towards useful creative tools.

Typically, you see "latent diffusion models". A VAE (Variational Autoencoder) compresses the input data into a smaller "latent space" and the diffusion model learns how to generate within this subspace.

Over the past few months, we've been publishing our work on efficient pixel-space diffusion models. These throw away the VAE, having the diffusion model learn a latent-space optimized for its exact task.

This serves 3 purposes: 1) Simplify Architecture (no 2-stage model training) 2) Faster Convergence (11x faster convergence vs. our latent diffusion counterpart) 3) Cheaper Inference (4x more aggressive token reduction in attention context-windows, without significant loss in quality)

This past month we were pressure testing our latest architecture (Pyramid-JiT) by training a text-to-image model longer than the typical one-off experiment. Specifically, we trained it for ~$20K on 660M samples.

We were surprised by the quality of results, so we thought we'd release it as open weights for the community (Apache 2.0). The research itself is already public, on our website.

For us, it's a big stepping stone towards cheaper video models, since pretty much all video models start as image models. We like to say these models have to learn nouns before they learn verbs.

title.value: Show HN: A decent text-to-image model trained for ~$20K (Apache 2.0 Weights)

story_text.value:
I came across some cool audio visuals on TikTok and wondered if I could send the video to Opus 5.5 and have it recreate it in a web interface.

One little POC led to adding a bunch of features with what is now a neat little way to take a break out of my day and just breath for a few minutes with a randomly generated piece of digital art.

I've had a few moments of serendipity when hitting the randomize button. Hope someone out there enjoys it.

It's mind boggling that you can just dream up stuff now and within a day have a cool little thing, even if its just yours.

story_text.value:
I have been posting on LinkedIn for more than 18 months and have had more than 4 million impressions.

The one thing it took me a while to understand is that there is not a single algorithm.

My belief is that the number of impressions highly depends on the one posting.

I made a web game based on this thesis.

You are shown real posts and have to guess the number of impressions.

I find it quite entertaining, but it also questions our beliefs about how platforms like LinkedIn and X work.

I will be available to answer all your questions and would be happy to hear your thoughts on the gameplay.

title.value: Show HN: 25posts – Guess the impressions of real LinkedIn posts

story_text.value:
Hi!

I made Meshword, a daily puzzle combining crosswords and nonograms.

Each row and column has groups of scrambled letters. You need to work out the words, where they fit, and which squares are blank. There’s a new puzzle each day, and 60 practice puzzles across Easy, Medium and Hard difficulty.

The app is built with Vue/Quasar, with PocketBase serving the puzzle catalog. I have been very happy with this stack across my various daily games.

Give it a try! Would love any feedback, especially related to puzzle difficulty, I am still fine-tuning that.

You can try it out on the website, or on iOS if you want the app lockout feature which lets you block your social apps. Completely free, with the option to support the app with a tip and unlock some additional icon and sharing options.

Coming soon is audio and auto-scroll, so you can set the phone down and read/listen hands free.

Android is on the way, the lockout feature is taking some additional review time.

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm a long-time Superhuman user, and a few weeks ago I cloned it as a native Mac app.

It's keyboard-first, with split inboxes, reminders, and a built-in calendar. It's local-first, including the AI features that use local models shipped in macOS 27, with the option to use Claude/Codex subscriptions. It's extremely configurable, even down to the search weights, and comes packed with CLI/MCP if you want to use it with an agent.

This is my daily driver for email, but it's by no means a "stable" product. Use at your own risk. I'm also working on a mobile app to go along with it.

Enjoy.
